title: 'Is this a cyberattack?' Grounded flights, a Microsoft outage and AI chaos fuel cybersecurity fears
summary: A series of unsettling disruptions, from tech stock turbulence and Microsoft outages to a nationwide grounding of flights, has left millions wondering whether the world’s increasingly interconnected technology systems are beginning to unravel.
author: FRANCE 24

title: Huang’s downfall shows human judgment is not all it’s cracked up to be
summary: The quality that sets us apart from machines has been absent during implosion by former Nvidia boss

title: Samsung conquered AI chips. Now it wants to build data centres
summary: South Korean conglomerate hopes to replicate success with semiconductors across its sprawling portfolio of businesses

title: Data centre construction stocks lose $4.2tn as boom in AI trade unravels
summary: Shares in AI ‘picks and shovels’ companies hit hard by tech sell-off

title: Arthur Mensch and Mistral AI: what does it take to keep a model in European hands?
summary: An organisation may want to run a powerful model close to the people whose records it processes. Mistral offers one route: release weights that can be deployed under the customer’s control, and sell the infrastructure and expertise needed to operate them. Arthur Mensch’s French company gives Europe a stake in frontier research. Its training hardware and industrial shareholders show how international that undertaking remains.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Zhilin Yang and Moonshot AI: who can promise capacity for Kimi?
summary: A subscription buys access to a model only while the service can answer. When demand for Kimi outstripped the available computing capacity, Moonshot paused new subscriptions. That episode illuminates founder Zhilin Yang’s two jobs. One is to improve a language model. The other is to secure the machines and capital to deliver it to the people who have paid for it.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Dayiheng Liu and Qwen: who steers the model inside Alibaba?
summary: A developer can download some Qwen models, rent others by the token and run either on infrastructure supplied by Alibaba. Three decisions lie behind that apparent choice. The researchers decide what to train, the cloud business decides what to sell and the parent company decides where capital goes. Dayiheng Liu’s career shows how much influence a technical leader can exercise within that structure and where his authority ends.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Alex Karp and the software between the model and the decision
summary: An AI supplier can shape a decision without training the model that produced the answer. Palantir links data, permissions and actions inside institutions. Alex Karp’s influence is easiest to see at the point where an analyst’s suggestion becomes something a hospital, factory or government agency can actually do.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Dario Amodei and the terms on which Anthropic can go public
summary: Anthropic promises to consider the long-term effects of the systems it builds. A proposed stock offering brings that promise into contact with shareholders seeking a return. Who can vote, who can appoint directors and who supplies the computing capacity each tell a different part of Dario Amodei’s story.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Elon Musk and the connection between satellites, servers and AI
summary: A customer can ask Grok a question over a Starlink connection. Parts of that journey now belong to the same listed group. Following the money from rockets and satellite subscriptions to servers explains why SpaceX belongs in a discussion about AI, and why its share price tells only part of the story.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Satya Nadella and Microsoft’s place on both sides of an AI purchase
summary: A company buying an AI assistant may already buy its office software, identity service and cloud capacity from Microsoft. Satya Nadella helped build the cloud business before he became chief executive. His position matters wherever a customer must decide how easily one part of that bundle can be replaced.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Sam Altman and the question of who controls OpenAI
summary: Who gets to appoint the board of a company that builds frontier AI? Sam Altman runs OpenAI, Microsoft owns an economic interest and a nonprofit holds governing rights. Following those three strands helps explain how a model can change a market without its chief executive owning that market.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Mark Zuckerberg and the votes behind Meta’s AI strategy
summary: A shareholder may own part of Meta and still have little say over the next generation of its AI. Mark Zuckerberg’s voting majority connects decisions about models, data centres and the distribution of information to one founder. The company’s public filings show exactly how that majority works.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Sundar Pichai and the routes through which Google brings AI to the public
summary: A model can reach millions before anyone chooses it by name. At Alphabet, Sundar Pichai oversees the researchers who build Gemini, the infrastructure that runs it and the products through which people encounter its answers. Google’s founders retain voting power that the chief executive himself does not possess.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Colette Kress and the board that chose NVIDIA’s interim chief
summary: When a founder leaves, who gets to choose a successor? At NVIDIA the answer arrived in a securities filing. The board appointed its finance chief, Colette Kress, to run the company while it searches for a permanent chief executive. It gave someone else the chair.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Should you invest in AI stocks now? Nvidia’s slump, Anthropic’s IPO and 5 strategies to consider
summary: Nvidia shares suffered their steepest weekly decline in more than 18 months, while Anthropic’s proposed IPO drew orders six times the available shares. The contrasting signals suggest investors are becoming more selective about AIQ

title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
summary: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
author: Connie Loizos

title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
summary: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...
author: Nick Robins-Early

title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.

title: Landing to Raw to Bronze or straight from Landing to Bronze?
summary: tl;dr: I am currently working on building my personal data lake and medallion + platinum pipeline and need help deciding whether to have an Landing zone to Raw to Bronze steps for ingesting data or go directly to Bronze from the Landing zone. Context: I am working on a quantfied_self project where i am collecting a bunch of data on myself. Things like (everything is timestamped): - Location at all points in the day, - Every single workout set - Major actions i do during a day like brushing teeth, reading a book, meals, work, socialising etc etc etc - Financial transactions - Hourly health metrics like heart rate, Hrv, steps, energy spent, calorie intake etc etc etc - And a lot of other data. Again everything is timestamped so can be watermarked easily. The plan: The plan is to build my own local data platform where i upload / send the data and it runs PySpark transformations on the data through a medallion architecture and i can use the gold/platinum datasets for visualisations and getting insights into my behaviour patterns. What I currently have: - An old laptop that i have converted to a ubuntu server (with GUI) to be used for storage and compute. - Samba is setup and I have automated data transfer to the exposed “incoming” folder using automations that can run automatically or on demand. - The repo is set up and a cron job inside the repo runs the pipelines on schedule on the server. - Current architecture: Data collection (csv or json) -> auto save via automations to “/incoming/health” or “/incoming/financial” or “/incoming/gps” etc etc folders. It works and I am happy to proceed with the next step which is ingestion. What i want to ask is: - Should the next step be “/incoming/*” -> “/raw/health”, “raw/workout”, “/raw/financial” folders, which would be an exact replica of the incoming folder for redundancy purposes or - Go straight to “/bronze/workouts” “/bronze/transactions” or “bronze/heart_rate” and skip raw since that will be one less step to manage??
